So, you're confusing a whole bunch of things here man.

  1. Power (watts) is not the same as power density (watts/cm^2). The original image describes the safety limits of the power density, as does OSHA guidelines. The original transmission power doesn't mean anything alone, you need the transmission power and the distance.
  2. 5Ghz is not the same as 5G. The link you posted in your 3rd point relates to the 5Ghz frequency transmission power guidelines.
  3. Cell phone wifi signals, and cellular signals, are completely different. The links you posted only apply to wifi bands as those are they are in the microwave range.
  4. Cell phones have a lower transmission power than routers. The max transmission power of a router is 1W, but the max on a cell phone is usually around .04 W (16.5 dBm). Transmitting a watt of power from a cell phone would drain the battery very quickly.
  5. Actual 5G frequencies have a max base station power of 75 dBm (31622 W), and device power of 43 dBm (19 W) per FCC guidelines. The idea here is that the base stations will be fewer and farther between, so the distance to them will be extremely far. The main issue then is the phone transmission power. The proposed max (19W) is the worst possible case, but in practice phones will be transmitting at about the same wattage they are now (~.04 W) due battery lifetime limitations.

So some math:

Let's use the guidelines in the first image, 10 mW/cm^2, as our safety threshold (though, note at the bottom is says it's unsafe when exposed to it for a long period of time), and a transmission power of 1W as the worst case (by law). The safe distance per the original image would be

10 mW/cm^2 = 1000 mW/(4pir^2 cm^2)

r = sqrt(100/(4*pi)) = 2.8 cm, or 1.1 inches

That means as long as you're farther than 1 inches from your router, you are well below the minimum safe power density (at a 1W transmission power). For a cell phone, this is even smaller, so there is absolutely no risk using the current bands.

Let's look at the proposed 5G maxes

Base station

10 mW/cm^2 = 31662000 mW/(4pir^2 cm^2)

r = sqrt(3166200/(4*pi)) = ~501 cm = 197 inches = 16 ft

Mobile

10 mW/cm^2 = 19000 mW/(4pir^2 cm^2)

r = sqrt(1900/(4*pi)) = ~ 12 cm = ~4 inches

So this definitely looks pretty bad at first, but consider the following. First, cell phone base stations are far above 16ft away from you (they're usually on high up), so that won't really affect anything (remember, power density falls of quadratically!). For mobile, there are two things to note. First, the 5G antennas must be directional per the spec, meaning that it will be pointing away from your face, versus the non-directional antennas used right now. Second, although 19W is the max, a typical phone is still going to use around the .04 W they do now (and actually can use less since the antennas are directional!). The power density in that case will be the same as it is now in the worse case, and will often be much less (unless you happen to be holding your phone to your head, and the base station is on the other side of you).
